title: Rehearsing and Varying Sentences
keyIdea: Rehearsing means saying your words aloud first, then putting it on paper. Saying it lets you try two or three versions and keep the best: a verb that fits the moment (crept, whispered, yelled), a conjunction that keeps the meaning (because, so, but, when) and inverted commas round only the words someone says. Clear beats long, and a mix of short sentences, joined sentences and dialogue keeps a reader interested.

kid: Say your words out loud first, then put it on paper. This is called rehearsing. When you hear it, you can tell if it sounds right. Then you can try it another way and pick the best one.

Try different words. The fox went across the garden. Is that the best word? Say crept, then stomped. Crept shows the fox is sneaking. Stomped would wake everyone up. Keep the word that fits what is happening.
Try different shapes too. Two short ideas can join with a conjunction: Mia put on her coat because she was cold. Because gives a reason. So gives a result. But shows a problem. When gives a time.

When someone talks, say their words in their voice first. Then write them inside inverted commas: "Let's go!" shouted Tom. Only the spoken words go inside, with the ! or ? too. A good story mixes short lines, joined lines and talk.
adult: The English National Curriculum asks Year 3 and 4 pupils to draft by composing and rehearsing sentences orally, including dialogue, and to build a varied and rich vocabulary and an increasing range of sentence structures. The grammar for these years adds conjunctions such as when, if, because and although, and inverted commas for direct speech. US Common Core L.3.1 and L.3.3 cover simple, compound and complex sentences and choosing words for effect.

Oral rehearsal works because a child can hold, test and change a line ahead of the slow work of handwriting and spelling. Ask for two or three versions of the same idea, said aloud, and talk about which one works best and why. The reason matters more than the choice.

Common mistakes: putting inverted commas round the whole line, including the reporting clause ('called Dad'); choosing an impressive verb that does not fit, such as 'thundered' for a sneaking mouse; using 'so' where the second clause is the reason; and piling up adjectives in the belief that longer is better. Watch too for a page where every line has the same shape.

In the lab your child marks the inverted commas in three lines of dialogue and tries verbs aloud for three moments. They join four pairs of ideas with because, so, but or when, and pick the clearest of three versions twice. Last, they rewrite a short story so it mixes a short line, a joined line and dialogue.

familyTip: At dinner, pick one thing that happened today and take turns saying it three different ways: a short version, a version joined with because or when, and a version with someone speaking. Vote on which one you would write down, and say why.

visual.caption: Short, joined or dialogue? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: We left early because it was snowing.
The bell rang, so we lined up.
I was hungry, but tea was not ready.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: mark dialogue, try verbs aloud, join ideas with conjunctions, pick the clearest version and mix sentence shapes.

practice.prompt: Why should you rehearse a sentence aloud before you write it, and try varying it?
choices: To hear if it sounds right and pick the best version
To make every sentence as long as possible
So you can skip the full stop
practice.hint: What can you notice when you hear a sentence out loud?
practice.explain: Saying it aloud lets you hear it, try another way and keep the version that works best. Long is not the aim, and full stops are still needed.

practice.prompt: Kai says his sentence aloud {n} times, with a different verb each time. He writes down only the best one. How many versions does he not use?
practice.hint: He keeps one version. Take that one away from the total.
practice.explain: He tried {n} versions and kept 1, so {=n-1} versions were not used. Trying them still helped him choose.

practice.prompt: Which line of dialogue is punctuated correctly?
practice.hint: Which words did Ravi actually say?
practice.explain: Ravi said "Is it time yet?", so only those words and the question mark go inside the inverted commas. "Asked Ravi" stays outside.

practice.prompt: A paragraph has {n} short sentences. Lily joins {k} pairs of them with because or so. How many sentences does the paragraph have now?
practice.hint: Each join turns two sentences into one, so each join takes away one sentence.
practice.explain: Each of the {k} joins turns two sentences into one, so {n} − {k} = {=n-k} sentences are left.

pool.prompt: A mouse is sneaking past a sleeping cat. Which verb fits best?
pool.hint: Say each one aloud. Which shows the mouse is being careful?
pool.explain: Tiptoed shows the mouse moving quietly. Thundered is loud, and went does not show sneaking at all.

pool.prompt: Which conjunction fits? "We stayed inside ___ it was raining."
pool.hint: Is the rain the reason or the result?
pool.explain: The rain is the reason, so because fits. So would make the rain a result of staying in, and but suggests a surprise.

pool.prompt: Which version sounds best in a story?
choices: The owl swooped down onto the field.
The big dark grey soft quiet owl went down very very fast.
The owl went. It went down. It went to the field.
pool.hint: Look for a strong verb and no pile of extra words.
pool.explain: Swooped is a strong verb that does the work. The second version piles up adjectives, and the third repeats went three times.

pool.prompt: Every line in Dan's story starts with "Then I". What is the best fix?
choices: Say some sentences aloud in new ways, such as with dialogue or a joining word
Write the same story more quickly
Add more sentences that start "Then I"
pool.hint: The problem is that every line has the same shape.
pool.explain: Rehearsing new versions aloud gives a mix of sentence shapes. Writing faster or adding more of the same does not fix it.

pool.prompt: A story has {n} sentences. {k} of them are dialogue. How many sentences are not dialogue?
pool.hint: Take the dialogue sentences away from the total.
pool.explain: {n} sentences take away {k} lines of dialogue leaves {=n-k} sentences that are not dialogue.

pool.prompt: Which words go inside the inverted commas? Mum said Come and eat
pool.hint: Inverted commas hold only the words that are spoken.
pool.explain: Mum spoke the words "Come and eat", so they go inside: Mum said, "Come and eat." The words Mum said stay outside.

pool.prompt: Asha tries {n} different openings for her idea aloud, then {k} more. How many versions has she tried?
pool.hint: Add the first tries and the extra tries.
pool.explain: {n} tries and {k} more make {=n+k} versions to choose from.

pool.prompt: Which sentence joins two clauses with a conjunction?
choices: The bell rang, so we lined up.
pool.hint: Look for a joining word such as so, because, but or when.
pool.explain: So joins "The bell rang" and "we lined up" into one sentence. The others are a short sentence and a line of dialogue.
